title: The health evidence advisers
subtitle: Design a club plan using science, access and honest claims
objective: Explain how diet, activity, drugs and daily routines can affect the body using a fictional club plan.

sow.exactOutcome: Explain the impact of diet, exercise, drugs and lifestyle on the body (links PSHE).
sow.alignment: Directly develops this stated outcome with secondary-age tasks at an upper-KS2 conceptual level. Support and stretch are flexible; this exemplar is not a claim of qualification approval.

priorLearning: Know that blood transports nutrients and oxygen.
success: Link a lifestyle factor to a body effect.
Explain that medicines can help when used as directed but also have risks.
Recommend an accessible plan without promising perfect health.

vocabulary.meaning: The overall pattern of food and drink a person has.
Body movement that uses energy; many activities can be adapted.
A substance that changes how the body works; medicines are examples.
The chance that something may happen, not a guarantee.
Information used to support or challenge an explanation.

equipment: Printed source and proposal cards, selected route, pencils.
preparation: Read all fictional club constraints. Avoid discussion of pupils’ weight, family habits, diagnoses or medicines.
No food tasting or movement trial is required; use desk planning.
safety: Do not ask pupils to disclose medication or advise anyone to stop or change prescribed medicine.
Use fictional profiles only. Follow existing school support procedures if a pupil voluntarily raises a personal concern.
All activities are paper-based; no smoke, alcohol, medicines or food samples are handled.
practicalAlternative: Use the supplied fictional club and short source cards. No personal records, exercise or internet access are needed.

misconceptions.claim: One food or activity guarantees health.
misconceptions.correction: Health has many influences; an action can support health without guaranteeing an outcome.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether a risk statement predicts every individual.

misconceptions.claim: All drugs are harmful and medicines should be stopped.
misconceptions.correction: Medicines can treat conditions when used as directed; they can also have side effects.
misconceptions.check: Ask who should advise about medicine use.

misconceptions.claim: Everyone can use exactly the same activity plan.
misconceptions.correction: Access, abilities, health needs and enjoyment differ; activity can be adapted.
misconceptions.check: Ask how to make a club option accessible.

access.supported: Match factor and effect; select a plan using sentence frames.
access.standard: Evaluate proposals and justify two linked changes.
access.stretch: Repair overclaims and balance evidence with access constraints.
access.regulation: Offer quiet pointing, private writing, drawing or adult scribing. Pass-and-return for public questions. Use fictional cases; no personal medical disclosure or comparison of bodies. Assign response routes from current evidence, not fixed pupil labels.

sources.title: NHS: The Eatwell Guide
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Varied eating patterns and different food groups; no food scoring, calorie prescription or individual diet plan.

sources.title: NHS: Physical activity for children and young people
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Accessible activity supports health; no compulsory exercise or pupil fitness assessment.

sources.title: WHO: Noncommunicable diseases
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Tobacco smoke, alcohol and other influences affect disease risk, not individual certainty or blame.

sources.title: NHS: Medicines A to Z
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Medicine information includes purpose, correct use and side effects. This lesson gives no medicine changes or dosage advice.

sources.title: NHS: Sleep and tiredness
sources.note: Checked September 2026. Sleep supports functioning; fictional routine design, no personal sleep data.

slides.title: A club asks for scientific advice
body: A fictional club wants a plan that supports bodies.
Which ideas have evidence and respect different needs?
slides.notes: Explain there is no pupil health questionnaire. Pupils advise the imaginary club, not themselves or classmates.

slides.title: Useful substances, useful evidence
body: R1. What carries oxygen around the body?
R2. Name a nutrient or food substance the body uses.
R3. Does “can help” mean “always guarantees”?
slides.notes: R1 blood; R2 carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamins, minerals or water. R3 no. Do not classify individual foods as good or bad.

slides.title: I connect a factor to a body effect
body: I name the factor: overall diet.
I explain the effect: supplying different nutrients.
I avoid judging a person from one meal.
slides.notes: Think aloud: I use “varied pattern” because bodies need different substances. Food access, allergies and culture matter. The diagram gives selected examples; foods contain mixtures of nutrients, and individual needs vary.

visual.title: Food patterns supply different needs
visual.description: Three parallel food-group examples show overlapping nutrient contributions: starchy foods provide carbohydrate, protein foods supply amino acids, and fruit or vegetables supply fibre and other nutrients. No transformation between groups is implied.

elements.text: Food patterns supply different needs

Starchy foods
provide carbohydrate

supply amino acids

Fruit / vegetables
provide fibre
and more

Food groups overlap. Variety over time matters;
this is not a list of good and bad people or foods.

slides.title: I explain an activity effect
body: During suitable activity, muscles usually need more oxygen.
Heart and breathing can speed up.
Regular suitable activity can support health.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Distinguish an immediate response from longer-term support. Say can support, not guarantees health or proves fitness. Movement may be seated, wheeled or otherwise adapted; this lesson requires none.

on paper; nobody must exercise for evidence.

slides.title: I treat drug claims carefully
body: Medicines change how the body works.
Helpful effects and side effects can both occur.
Scientific advice respects proper directions.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Model: “All drugs are bad” is too broad. Medicines can help treat a condition when used as directed. A lesson cannot tell someone to stop treatment. Smoke and harmful alcohol use have risks; discussing risks does not judge people.

visual.title: Medicines: purpose, directions and effects
visual.description: Three parallel considerations for medicine use: intended benefit, correct directions and possible side effects. These are not a causal sequence.

Use prescribed medicines as directed.

slides.title: The adviser board
body: Use source cards A–F and proposals P–S.
W1. Keep, adapt or reject each proposal.
Give one evidence-card reason.
slides.notes: P/Q/R can be kept with access conditions; S reject as unsafe unqualified advice. Cards supply all facts. Invite teams or private written adjudication.

table.caption: Proposals are constructed classroom scenarios, not medical advice.

slides.title: Design for access
body: W2. Choose two proposals to combine.
Explain a body effect and an access adjustment.
Food is represented by cards; no tasting.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. P+Q, P+R or Q+R can all work if justified. Example P+Q: varied nutrients plus suitable movement; allergy-aware cards and quiet/seated options. There is no single healthiest person or compulsory activity.

slides.title: The exaggerated poster
body: Poster: “Our club guarantees nobody will get ill.”
W3. Repair it using “can support” and a reason.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. Model after pupils: Our varied, accessible plan can support health, but many influences affect illness and no plan guarantees nobody becomes ill. No blame for illness.
slides.reveal: This plan can support health. It cannot guarantee an individual outcome.

slides.title: A medicine has possible side effects
body: Which statement is scientifically responsible?
slides.notes: A unsafe and overgeneralised. B correct. C falsely guarantees no risk. Revisit benefits/directions/side effects diagram.

options.feedback: A class cannot direct someone to stop treatment. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber.

options.text: It may help when used as directed; ask a professional about concerns.
options.feedback: This recognises intended benefits, directions and possible risks.

options.text: If it is a medicine, it can never cause harm.
options.feedback: Medicines can have side effects and incorrect use can cause harm.

slides.title: Write the club recommendation
body: Choose one response route.
Use the source cards to explain body effects.
Include access and one honest limit.
slides.notes: 10 minutes across You do. All routes cover diet, activity and drug/routine effects. A dictated recommendation is valid.

slides.title: Link, do not list
body: “We suggest ____ because ____.”
“People can take part by ____.”
“This does not prove ____.”
slides.notes: Shared time. Ask for a specific physiological or functional effect rather than “it is healthy” alone.

slides.title: Check your wording
body: Have I explained effects on the body?
Have I avoided personal judgement?
Have I kept medicine decisions with professionals?
slides.notes: Shared time. No calorie targets, body measurements or weight goals. Replace guarantees with bounded claims.

slides.title: Evidence before a slogan
body: Share one scientific reason.
A partner or teacher checks its source card.
Improve an overclaim if needed.
slides.notes: 4 minutes across Review. Evidence can be spoken privately. Separate a source supporting a broad health relation from proof of an individual outcome.

slides.title: Which access change should we show?
body: Suggest an accessible way to join the fictional club.
Choose one to add to the final class plan.
slides.notes: Lundy: teacher adopts a justified accessible option and explains how pupils’ input changed the plan. No vote about whose body or lifestyle is better.

slides.title: Three responsible science statements
body: E1. Give a diet–body link.
E2. Give an activity–body link.
E3. Explain one medicine precaution.
slides.notes: Diet supplies different nutrients; activity can support heart/muscles/bones or increase oxygen delivery during movement; take medicines as directed and ask professional about concerns. E4 on page: can support does not guarantee.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: adviser board
pupilPages.intro: Short paraphrases of NHS and WHO guidance. P–S are fictional proposals: P varied food cards/water; Q adapted optional movement/quiet alternative; R calm routine/smoke-free space; S stop everyone’s medicine.

cards.title: A • Food patterns | NHS
cards.text: Different food groups supply different nutrients. A varied overall pattern supports the body; a single snack does not define someone’s health.

cards.title: B • Movement | NHS
cards.text: Regular suitable activity supports heart, muscle and bone health. Activities can be adapted for access and enjoyment.

cards.title: C • Smoke and alcohol | WHO
cards.text: Tobacco smoke and harmful alcohol use can damage body systems and increase disease risk. Risk is not certainty or a judgement of a person.

cards.title: D • Medicines | NHS
cards.text: Medicines can help treat conditions. Directions and side effects matter. Ask a pharmacist or prescriber; do not change treatment in this task.

cards.title: E • Rest | NHS
cards.text: Sleep and rest support daily functioning. Calm routines can help, although people do not control every barrier to sleep.

cards.title: F • Fictional club brief
cards.text: Offer choices and respect allergies, culture and access. No purchases or personal health data. The hall and a quiet room are available; food is represented by cards.

blocks.prompt: W1. Keep, adapt or reject P–S. Give one source-card reason.
W2. Combine two useful proposals. Explain one body effect and an access adjustment.
W3. Repair “Our club guarantees nobody will get ill.”

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: choose and explain
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1; no personal health details are needed.

blocks.prompt: S1. Which supplies a range of nutrients?
choices: Judging a person from one snack

blocks.prompt: S2. Complete: Suitable activity can help ____ and ____ . Word bank: heart / muscles / guarantee no illness.
S3. What should the club do about prescribed medicines?
choices: Keep to directions; questions go to a professional

blocks.prompt: S4. Choose P, Q or R. Explain one body effect and one way to include different needs.
S5. Finish: This plan can support health, but it cannot ____ .

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: club recommendation
pupilPages.intro: Use source-card letters to support your reasons.

blocks.prompt: N1. Complete the table with a scientific link for each factor.
N2. Recommend two proposals P–R. Explain why and add one access adjustment.
N3. Explain why proposal S should be rejected.
N4. Improve the guarantee poster. Include a routine or rest idea and a limit.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: evidence and limits
pupilPages.intro: Write clear science for a mixed group without giving individual medical instructions.

blocks.prompt: T1. Explain diet, activity and smoke/alcohol effects using source cards. Distinguish a short-term response from a longer-term risk or benefit.
T2. Design a club plan from P–R with two explicit access adjustments and scientific reasons.
T3. Explain why “all drugs harm” and “medicines never harm” are both inaccurate.
T4. Could a successful club session prove nobody will develop illness? Explain a limit and a better claim.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Exit and reflection
pupilPages.intro: Use the fictional club; no personal disclosure.

blocks.prompt: E1. Explain one connection between diet and the body.
E2. Explain one connection between activity and the body.
E3. Give one responsible precaution about medicines.
E4. Why is “can support health” different from “guarantees health”?
Reflection. Which access adjustment would improve the club plan?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: Blood; an appropriate nutrient or water; no, can help is not certainty.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 keep/adapt P, Q and R using A/B/C/E/F; reject S using D. W2 accept any two useful proposals with accurate body links and an access adjustment such as allergy-aware choices, seated/wheeled options or quiet participation. W3 replace guarantee with can support health; many factors affect illness.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A incorrect: stopping everyone’s medicine is not justified. B correct: follow directions and consult a pharmacist/prescriber about concerns. C incorrect: side effects and risks exist.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 varied pattern. S2 heart and muscles (bones also valid). S3 keep to directions/professional questions. S4 P nutrients and accessible choices, Q activity benefits and adaptation, or R rest/smoke exposure and quiet options. S5 guarantee that nobody becomes ill.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: N1 diet supplies nutrients/A; activity supports heart/muscle/bone/B; tobacco smoke/harmful alcohol can damage systems or increase disease risk/C; medicine can help treat conditions but directions/side effects matter/D. N2 any justified P–R pair and access adjustment. N3 unqualified blanket treatment change could cause harm. N4 calm routine/rest may support functioning; plan cannot guarantee no illness.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 accurate factor/effect links: e.g. during activity muscles need more oxygen and heart usually speeds up; regular suitable activity supports health over time. Tobacco/alcohol risk is not certainty. T2 scientifically justified combination with two distinct access adjustments. T3 medicines are drugs with possible benefits and unwanted effects. T4 a single session cannot establish long-term outcomes or remove all causes of illness; “the plan can support health and access” is defensible.

answers.label: E1–E4 / reflection
answers.answer: E1 varied diet supplies different nutrients. E2 suitable activity supports body systems or immediate increased oxygen delivery. E3 use as directed; consult pharmacist/prescriber about concerns. E4 support changes chances or functioning, not a guaranteed individual outcome. Reflection: accept a reasoned access change.

answers.label: Assessment and re-teach
answers.answer: Secure: explains at least one diet link, one activity link and one drug effect/precaution, with an inclusive bounded recommendation. Re-teach vague healthy labels by completing factor→body effect. Correct moral judgement, guarantee claims and treatment-change advice immediately and calmly.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.
All profiles and proposals are fictional. Health is affected by social conditions, environment and chance as well as actions; illness must not be framed as moral failure.
Use drug as a scientific category including medicines. Avoid named recreational drug effects, doses or personal questioning; the taught scope is broad body effects and responsible evidence.
Interactive We do: pupils predict, test the diagram and explain. Paper equivalent is W1–W3 with source cards; it reaches the same decisions without animation.

interactive.title: Adviser board: choose, test, improve
interactive.intro: Predict first, test the model, then explain using the evidence. Move at your own pace; paper W1–W3 tasks assess the same reasoning.
